title: Shishobo - A Bodhisattva's Embracing Method of Guidance
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach shares insights from Dogen's teachings, specifically the concept of generosity (dana), which is one of the four methods of guidance in Buddhism. Generosity is not just about giving material objects, but also about cultivating a mindset of openness and acceptance, allowing oneself to receive and appreciate what is given without expectation or attachment. By practicing generosity, individuals can release themselves from the three poisons of greed, hate, and delusion, and cultivate a deeper sense of compassion and wisdom.

sentences.text: Good evening everyone.
Thank you for coming the day after a holiday that's hot and inviting.
This marks the first of four lectures that will be given by senior students here.
Many of you know that our task this year has been to enter into Dogen Zenji's teachings in different ways, so I think each of us is planning to talk on Dogen's writings in some way.
In a way I feel very much at home with this, and in a way daunted.
I'm a bit of what you might call a Dogen nerd.
I've been studying Dogen with a great deal of intensity with someone who specializes, if you will, in the translations and commentary on Dogen's writings in the Shobogenzo.
Since not all of us know what that is, let me back up a little and say a few words about it.
But first I want to say this talk is a bit of an experiment.
Normally talks on a Wednesday are public talks.
They're meant to encourage you in some aspect of the Dharma, so you walk out feeling like, wow, this is my life.
I can do this.
I want to do this.
I really feel called and supported by the Dharma.
I'm taking a risk because I'm going to do it a little differently than I normally do.
I'm going to take this as a study hour together.
We have a full hour for this.

In my many years of studying with Shohaku Okumura, there's a particular style he uses to teach Dogen, and out of respect and gratitude for him I wanted to share a little about how I've studied Dogen, so it'll be a little different.

Dogen Zenji is the founding teacher of this lineage of Zen, the Japanese monk who went from Japan to China and brought back the true Dharma that became Soto Zen, which is this particular lineage in Japan.
He's a very important person, and I'll say a little more about why he made such a big splash and why we remember him.
In fact, we chant the Buddhas and ancestors every Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday at the Berkeley Zen Center, which is where I did most of my training.
I remember when I didn't know the ancestors at all and I didn't know much of anything, we'd be going through this long list of probably about 40 or 50 names, and then we'd get to Dogen.
Everyone's voices would get really strong and powerful with enthusiasm.
So I always wondered who this guy Dogen was.
The Shobogenzo is his masterwork.

Depending upon who you believe and how you count them, there are somewhere between 75 and 89 or 92 different writings that go in the Shobogenzo, each of which really is a different kind of love song to Zazen, but in different kinds of ways.
I'm going to talk on one in particular, and I'm going to use a lot of Okumura's words and a lot of Dogen's words just to give you a taste.
Then I'll thread in a few of my own.
And we have a full hour for this, which is a great opportunity.
I have no idea how long this is going to run, but I think it'll be well less than an hour.
My hope, much as with the July series we did last year, is that everyone will notice that something's arisen for them.
A disagreement: that's not how I understand the Dharma.
A question.
An opening of the heart or the mind.
Something that just comes up for you, so that we all will have something we might want to say.
Then if we have any time left, maybe we'll do it as an open discussion where everyone just offers up as they want to.
We'll see what comes up.
I truly and sincerely hope you'll say whether this was a useful way of hearing the Dharma.
It's not the usual teisho.

One of Okumura's ways of teaching that I have found very rewarding is that he's a translator, so he'll look at the kanji and talk about all the different words that a particular character can represent, and he'll talk about why he chooses a particular character.
In doing so you get to examine what the true meaning is.
What was Dogen trying to say and why was he trying to say it?
What makes sense?
We'll do a little of that.
I also want to place this fascicle of Shobogenzo in its historical place.
We often read the Dharma and we just take from it where we are now, and that's very good.
That's our nourishment.
But as we study it more deeply, it's very helpful to understand how it arose in its time.
Why was he saying this?
What was going on at that time?
We understand more deeply some of the factors, and that can be useful too.
I think of Dogen as being rather like the Nobel laureate of philosophy and literature, with Pulitzer Prizes in poetry and prose.
If you've ever tried to read him, you know how complicated he is.
Much as Norman enjoys playing with words and using words to reveal something more deeply that you can't see in words, Dogen's a master at it.
When Dogen does it, each sentence has a meaning even though, when you put them all together, it seems like they contradict each other.
But he really is saying something powerful, powerfully different.
It's really meant to explode your ideas about things.
You're not meant to understand it in a cognitive way, although you can approach it that way.
We say in Soto Zen that we don't study koans, those kinds of unanswerable questions and stories, like they do in Rinzai, but actually that's all Dogen is.
It's a bunch of koans, sentence by sentence.
The other thing we don't really appreciate so much about Dogen is that he wrote in Chinese, he wrote in Japanese, and he wrote in colloquial Japanese.
He was taking the same words and phrases in a sentence and a paragraph, using three different languages, and playing with it.
A translator is trying to get that essence when they offer it up.
So he really is being a complete poet, masterfully playful in what he says.
It's playing with language in the same way we think of Suzuki Roshi as being kind of quaint and also very deep.
For example, when he says "things as it is," we go, no, no, no, that's not proper grammar.
But when you study Zen, "things as it is" actually means the total arising of everything interacting with each other, arising in this moment, produces this, just this moment.
Dogen does the same thing, and we can't fully get that, probably.
Okay, that's the background.
Are you bored yet?
No?
Just raise your hands when you are.
Good luck.
The fascicle of Dogen I want to talk on is Shishobo.
Have you ever studied Shishobo?
Shishobo is the Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance, and it was my first introduction to Zen, actually.
Uh-oh, is someone else doing that?
Well, we have a couple of weeks to pick something else.
No, because I'm going to do it in one style and you're going to do it in the other style.
The truth is I'm only planning to do the very first section of it.
I'm not going to do all of it tonight.
So maybe I won't be.
That's John and Chris?
Oh, good.
This is great, because I thought, oh, this is too bad, I'm not going to get through all of it.
So, Shishobo is the 26th fascicle and it was written in 1243.
I found this really interesting: 1343 was the last year that Dogen was in Kyoto.
When he came back from China, he went back to his home temple for a little while.
It was really clear he had the itch to do something on his own.
What he learned was different enough from his old monastery that he took off to the south of Kyoto and opened his own temple, Koshoji.
He was there about ten years when this fascicle was written, on the fifth day of the fifth month, during the summer practice period.
Two months later, they were gone.
Two months later, that monastery was shut down.

They left almost in the middle of the night, or so it seems, and headed up north to Echizen, where Dogen happened to have a benefactor who had land and offered him the opportunity to come up with his students.
I think there were somewhere between 10 and 20 of them at that point in time.
We don't know exactly why they took off so suddenly.
Maybe that doesn't matter so much, but probably there were political pressures from the old monastery, from the Tendai monastery, where the abbot had connections with a very powerful emperor.
Somehow Dogen and his work had fallen in disfavor.
We don't know exactly why.
We probably never will.
This is the leading theory.
They just took off.
They really had no place to settle.
The cook cooked in a little house down a steep mountainside from where the monastery was.
You can imagine, every meal served up, the tenzo having to lug all the pots up the hill.
It was really only, I think, a couple of years later that they were settled in what was eventually named Eiheiji, which is still one of the home monasteries for our lineage.
I kind of mused, and it may be because some of us are studying precepts now, how much of this had something to do with his teaching of precepts, which are a little radical.
I bring it up because I think of Shishobo.
We'll get to what the title is and dissect it a little bit, but it's really about how a bodhisattva acts in the world.
What are the ways in which a bodhisattva, what's a bodhisattva?
A bodhisattva is someone like you who wants to help other people, wants to help bring them across the shore from the usual human world of suffering to a place where they have freedom.
These precepts in our Mahayana tradition have a history of how they evolved, and then Dogen took it a step forward.
In Shishobo, in my way of seeing it, he's talking about what the true activity of a bodhisattva is, what that quality is.
He names four qualities, which we'll touch on, but he's really talking about the spirit of that activity.

To give you a little background in precepts, and I'll tell you it can take Okumura Roshi two lectures to actually start talking about the fascicle, but just to give you some sense of putting it in a context: Dogen had his original training when he was 13, after his mother died and his father was gone.
He entered the Tendai monastery at age 13.

The Chinese Buddhist order, emerging without access to the Vinaya, which was the real traditional code of ethics or behavior that was in the Buddha's original monasteries and exists in India and Sri Lanka and some other places, had to develop its own interpretation of the Vinaya to gain legitimacy and acceptance by the Chinese government.
In Japan, however, Buddhist institutions were incorporated into the very first law codes, and the Vinaya was one of the six fields of learning officially promoted by the early Japanese court.
So the Japanese emperor said, you have to practice the Vinaya.
Don't ask me why, I don't know that history, but that was part of the rules.

When Saicho in the 1700s fought for, and succeeded in establishing, the Tendai school, which was Dogen's first school, he rejected the Vinaya, and he conducted ordinations based solely on the Mahayana principles, solely on these ideas of the bodhisattva activity: the idea of form is emptiness, emptiness is form, this idea that there is the relative, there's the absolute in the relative, and relative in the absolute all the time.
We live our world on this plane, but there's a much larger, unknown, and interconnected way in which things are related, and we need to understand all of those.
By rejecting ordinations based on the Vinaya, that meant that lay people and clergy took the same precepts.
They took the same precepts, so there was a leavening there, and that was pretty threatening to the Japanese emperor.
They didn't like the Tendai.
Then Dogen comes back from Japan, and he has even more radical ideas.
He simplifies the precepts further, makes them into the 16 that we take in all of our ceremonies.
We'll take them on the first Wednesday of next month.
We take them for lay ordinations, priest ordinations, marriages, funerals.
We take them for everything, those 16 precepts.
So that's how Dogen cut his teeth, and those are the only precepts he had taken when he got on the boat to China.
Guess what?
He wasn't allowed off the boat in China initially.
He hadn't taken all the precepts, and he was not allowed to practice as a full monk in China.
He had to sit in a different part of the hall where the lay people sat.
Isn't that interesting?
I think so.
So he's asking this question: what are these precepts really about?
What really matters about them?
They make such a big deal of this Vinaya in China.
What's really their essence to me?
So he comes back, and he writes his own.
And then somehow there's something going on with the Tendai monastery in Japan, and he has to leave not long after he delivers this talk on the Shobogenzo.
So bodhisattvas we have traditionally thought of as being like Buddha, right?
Buddha lived through many, many lifetimes, and he was a bodhisattva each time.
One time he gives up his body.
In fact, I don't remember these stories so well, but one time he gives up his body to a hungry lion, and another time isn't he a bird or something and sacrifices his life.
Each time he's doing something of enormous help to another and is reborn as another bodhisattva until he finally becomes the Buddha.
We also think of bodhisattvas as the embodiments of great particular kinds of energies or qualities.
Avalokiteshvara with compassion, Manjushri with wisdom, Jiso as a deeply compassionate accompaniment of people who are in trouble or who have died, Maitreya as the future bodhisattva.
But bodhisattva, just to say it again, means every single one of you in this room acting in your life.
These are your methods of guidance.
The title Shishobo: shi means four, that's easy.
Sho can mean embracing, unifying, integrative.
It's from shoju, which means to embrace or to accept.
So you can imagine we have slightly different turnings depending on which of those you take.

Different titles include the four methods of guidance, the foundations of social unity (that's actually very common in the Thai forest tradition), the foundations of social unity when you think about these qualities and what they mean, social unity.
The ways of showing favor, that's loaded, isn't it?
What does it mean to show favor?
The four integrated methods: what are you integrating?
What does it mean to embrace, unify, integrate?
Ho, which is the same as bo, ho means dharma.
It can mean something specific like things, unifying, embracing, all of these things, all of these objects.
It can mean the teaching.
So when we think about the four methods of guidance, we usually think about the guidelines, like with the precepts.
I think these point more to the quality of the pure precepts: avoid evil, do all that is good, live and be lived for the benefit of beings.
The specifics of how we manifest the Eightfold Path are the grave precepts.
I won't kill, I'll affirm life, I won't take what's not given, I will be generous.
These are a manifestation, these four methods of guidance.
Another way of looking at it though is by emphasizing the idea of embracing, the all-embracing activity of a bodhisattva.
When you really see an embrace, who's holding and who's being held?
Who's doing the holding?
Everyone's doing the holding.
Who's being held?
Everyone's being held.
Think about this in terms of holding and being held, the all-embracing method of guidance.
Menzan, who was a great translator of Dogen in Japan in the 18th century, early 19th century, really revived Dogen.
After he had been lost, Shobogenzo had been locked away somewhere.
He says:
*When a bodhisattva wishes to guide living beings and transform them, then without fail, she or he should embrace and accept living beings and allow them to trust him or her.
Then he or she guides them to the true Mahayana.*
In the Vimalakirti Sutra it said that we attract living beings with what they desire and then we enable them to enter Buddha's wisdom.
We attract them with what they desire, the aid that they need, the kindness that they need, the help that they need, and the encouragement not to feel alone but to know that they're connected.
So what Dogen is really teaching here is dana.
I should say the four methods of guidance are generosity or offering, loving words, beneficial action, and identity action.
I'm only going to talk about generosity tonight, hopefully.
But what Dogen is really teaching is dana-embracement, loving words-embracement, beneficial action-embracement, and identity action-embracement.
So when Dogen Zenji expounds these four practices in Shobogenzo, as Okumura Roshi says, he does not merely mean that these are methods of guiding people to enter the Buddhist path.
He teaches these four practices to allow us, ourselves, to be free from the three poisons of greed, hate, and delusion.
And to quote from him, I thought this was really beautiful.
This is a nice little book that my big Dharma brother, Alan Senauke, wrote.
When he talks about generosity as the first of the four methods of guidance, he says:
*Giving begins with oneself.
I give myself to practice, and practice offers itself to me.
In my search for peace, I find there is always a pervasive smell of war.
The taste of tears, corrosive doubt, and decay fall within the circle of my own body and mind.
A war goes on here, right where I hide behind a mask of self-attachment.
If I hide out in a shelter of privilege, I cut myself off from others.
True giving is receiving the gift of zazen mind and passing it to others in words and deeds.
It's not meant for hiding.*
So when we practice the four methods of guidance, we're saving ourselves as well as saving others.
Generosity in Japanese, fuse, which also means almsgiving, is the first of the paramitas.
The paramitas are the methods of enlightenment or deep wisdom, and the first of all of them is generosity, is giving.
Dogen starts Shishobo, and asks for a little more water.
I think it's so hot.
My throat's dry.
Listen to these words.
When Dogen writes a fascicle, really the first sentence or two, maybe the first paragraph, is the whole thing.
Everything else is commentary.
So if you're wondering what he's doing here, go back to the beginning.
This is the very beginning.
*Offering means not to be greedy.
Not to be greedy means not to covet.
Not to covet commonly means not to flatter.
There you are.
Even if we rule the four continents, to offer teachings of the true way, we must simply and unfailingly not be greedy.
It is like offering treasures we are about to discard to those we do not know.
We give flowers blooming on the distant mountains to the tathagata and offer treasures accumulated in past lives to living beings.
Whether our gifts are dharma or material objects, each gift is truly endowed with the virtue of offering or dharma.
Even if this gift is not our personal possession, nothing hinders our practice of offering.
No gift is too small, but our effort should be genuine.*
So not to covet means, thank you very much, not to covet means not to take anything as ours, not to feel possessive of it, not to run after it, feel like it's so important.
To practice dana is to be released from greed.
I think of this as the kind of coveting: everyone's seen Lord of the Rings or has some relation to it.
Is it Smagle?
Smagle, who's the one who wanted the ring?
Anything.
He'd do anything to have that ring, no matter what.
Yes.
Deep in our hearts somewhere we covet something.
Sometimes we covet a little bit, like, whatever it is, that special meal you're going to have on a nice, hot day on your porch.
That extra thing for your house that you just want to decorate it and make it kind of nice.
The car you've always, we have these little things that we really want.
Maybe you don't.
I do.
I get really focused.
Okay, this becomes really important.
I want to get this.
I really see this when I'm traveling.
I think, oh, that's really the best thing I get at home.
And I go, what?
To covet is not to be greedy.
I don't need that.
This person, to be happy, doesn't need this.
Flattering is another expression of greed.
Do you notice that way, how flattering is like greed?
Right?
You don't feel like you can get it on your own.
Why do you flatter someone?
You want to curry favor, right?
You want to be in a favorable light.
Maybe you need a good recommendation.
Maybe you want a cut in line.
Maybe you want someone to like you.
You want something.
Flattering is flattering.
You're not just being kind or observing, but you're actually trying to connect in a way where you're expecting something back from that person.
Whether you're just trying to ask them out for a date or something else, you're wanting something.
That's being greedy.
I want something from me.
I want something from you.
From me.
And it's interesting that Dogen uses the negative of dana to express it, right?
You don't usually think of dana in terms of I need not to be greedy.
But actually, I think what he's pointing at here is that he is asking us to look at the more subtle workings of our mind.
Practicing dana is one of the antidotes to one of the three poisons, the three poisonous minds, greed, hate, and delusion.
Generosity is an antidote for greed.
But it's a little facile sometimes just to give things, because you can still want something when you give things.
I want a tax deduction.
I want someone to think I'm a good person.
I want something in exchange from you.
I want a tax code rewritten in my favor.
Whatever it is, you want something in exchange sometimes.
But to be really invited to look at what am I wanting, when you say don't be greedy, don't covet, don't flatter: what am I wanting in here?
What's your deeper motivation?
I am going to skip the next section because I see I'm running on a little bit too long.
Maybe I'll say just a few words.
When I was in Japan and practicing there in the monastery, we did takahatsu.
Takahatsu is where you go out begging.
When you go out begging, you put on all your layers of robes.
You put on handmade straw sandals on your bare feet, no matter how hot, cold, muddy, rainy, whatever.
You go from door to door knocking and chanting.
You chant asking for a donation.
The donation is usually food.
It can be money.
It's used to support the monastery.
It's a very interesting exercise in just accepting what's given and not wanting anything.
Because sometimes people will slam the door in your face.
Sometimes they'll run away.
Sometimes they'll put something in and bow with such reverence to you.
And you go, oh my God, I don't deserve this.
And you wonder, who's this person?
You look in the bowl: is it something you want?
Is it good enough?
Is it too nice?
It's very hard practice just to receive what's put in your bowl, and not think either that you're not worthy of it, you're not good enough, or that you should have gotten something else.
But just to accept it for the sake of the Dharma.
You're just out there practicing because you're practicing the Dharma.
And by doing this, other people, the people who are putting something in the bowl or making the choice that they can make or want to make that day, are practicing the Dharma.
You're all turning the Dharma wheel.
And when you get an offering, you chant.
Oh, I didn't write it down.
There's a chant that says, thank you so much for this.
When you give this to me, you benefit the entire Dharma world.
And wishing blessings.
And when you don't get anything, you still chant a blessing.
The great Japanese poet Ryokan was well-known for going out on takahatsu rounds and losing himself completely, playing with children or collecting flowers.
He captures this spirit of just offering and just receiving in this poem.
*Playing ball with the children in this village, spring day, never let the shadow fall.
I was on my way to beg, but passing by a spring field, spent the whole day picking violets.
In my begging bowl, violets and dandelions are mixed together.
Let's make an offering to all the Buddhas in the three times.*
No offering too big, too small.
So that leads us to more about the nature of the gift.
Dogen says:
*It's like offering treasures we're about to discard to those we do not know.
We give flowers blooming on the distant mountains to the Tathagata and offer treasures accumulated in past lives to living beings.
Whether our gifts are of the Dharma or of material object, each gift is truly endowed with the virtue of offering or dana.*
Even if the gift is not our personal possession, nothing hinders our practice from offering.
Our mind is pure.
It doesn't get in the way of just offering what there is, offering flowers on the mountainside to the Tathagata.
When you see flowers when you're hiking up on Mount Baker now, the mountain's just filled with wildflowers, isn't it?
It's just so beautiful.
At least it was a couple of weekends ago.
Give those flowers to the Tathagata.
You just see them.
There's no thought that they're yours.
There's no thought that you're going to run and collect them and put them on your table.

But they're so beautiful, your heart opens in joy and in celebration of the natural beauty of the world, the natural expression, if you will, of the Buddha Dharma, which is the way things are, that you have joy.
You offer it back.
You give it right back, right?
You might take a picture and show someone.
You might go home and plant some, but actually you just offer it back up in joy.
That's the spirit of offering, like giving flowers on the mountainside to the Tathagata.
There's a marvelous book, Lewis Hyde's *The Gift*.
Has anyone read *The Gift*?
Yes.
The spirit of the gift: the gift is beyond the object or the thing.
It's an attitude, a spirit, a sense of generosity that's extended and is limitless as long as the gift keeps moving.
The gift has to keep moving.
You don't take it and hold onto it as your own.
Perhaps you have it for a while, and then someone else needs it.
Or it's just obvious that this is where it goes, and you pass it along.
I was talking with a patient today who came to me and said, "I'm an anthropologist.
I've collected things, particularly Buddhist things, from all over the world.
I'm getting older.
I don't know what to do with these precious things."
And I said, let them tell you.
Let them tell you where they go.
Just be with them.
They'll have another home.
We know how good that feels.
Some of you have heard me talk about the Tibetan monk that I saw in Bogaya when I was studying with the Dalai Lama, passing the same beggar every day.
I passed the same beggar every day.
It was so hard to look at him, this lama.
I gave him a coin, and the exchange of looks between those two people, I couldn't tell who got what.
Seriously.
I'm sure the beggar needed the coin.
I'm sure the lama gave him something.
I don't know whether it was big or small, but what they got was this electric connection that's giving to you right now.
We don't know who our benefactors are.
We don't know where their gifts came from.
My birth father told me a story one time of how he was in Nazi-occupied Greece when he was lined up with other people who didn't live in the village, and one of them was about to be shot.
He was the youngest.
He was about to be shot.
The man next to him dropped his cigarette case intentionally.
He got shot.
That man brought me here today.
He gave me a gift.
You don't know who your benefactors are.
That's how the gift works.
You don't know.
You just trust in the power of the turning of the wheel of dana, and that gives you the encouragement to do that of your own spirit.
I think I've probably talked longer than I had any intention to, and although I'm not quite done, maybe that's enough for one day.
Let me just leave you with one more Ryokan poem.
Let me leave you with two more little pieces with a tiny bit of commentary.
A line that we often hear of Dogen's comes from this section of Shishobo.
It is:
*When the way is entrusted to the way, we attain the way.*
When we really practice with the mind of just an open hand and not holding on to anything, we have a clear understanding of what our life is, to paraphrase it.
We offer ourselves to ourselves, and we offer others to others.
We offer ourselves to ourselves.
Take yourself completely.
Embrace yourself completely, is what [unclear: "Alan Sinaki"] was saying.
Take all of it.
Don't leave any part of it out.
It's all yours.
Give all of your life to yourself.
Don't hold anything back.
Not pain, not mistakes, not difficulties.
Receive it all.
Give yourself completely to yourself.
Give others to others.
Allow them to be themselves.
Don't have any idea of who they are.
Allow them to be who they are in this moment.
You come to them with an open mind and curiosity.
Allow them to be themselves.
Give yourself to yourself and others to others.
This is a lifetime of examination, just that phrase.
And finally, maybe we'll just end with one last poem from Ryokan.
He says:
*With no mind, the flower invites the butterfly.
With no mind, the butterfly visits the flower.
When the flower opens, the butterfly visits.
When the butterfly visits, the flower opens.
I also don't know him, and he also doesn't know me.
Without knowing, the principle of the emperor of heaven,*
meaning the Buddha Dharma, the workings of the way, the workings of life.
So I don't know him.
He doesn't know me.
We just meet like a butterfly and a flower.
Just meet.
That's the gift of Dharma.
So we have about ten minutes.
Imagine that you have some thoughts, some feelings, some reactions, some experiences.
I think you're lucky.
Maybe we don't have enough time to go around the room tonight, but I'd really like to hear if you have thoughts, unsettledness, insights, other experiences.
So please, speak and share your experiences.
Offer.
There are three kinds of giving: material giving, giving of the Dharma, and fearlessness.
And you can do all of that just in what you're saying here.
You can offer something specific, your practice of the Dharma, and you can be fearless by speaking and offering it in front of all people.
Please.

**Participant:** When you were talking about walking with the bull from door to door and the sea, it made me think of, I'm not walking from door to door, but it made me think of receiving my family and my ancestors on a daily basis.
Just look at this life force that comes through me, no matter the circumstances, no matter lots of pain and suffering, all of our stories, right?
There are deeper and deeper layers for me to keep receiving and just giving thanks to that again and again.
I'm amazed at the depth of it.
So that came up for me.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Yeah, beautiful.
You don't know what that all opens up to.
It just keeps revealing itself to you.
That's great.
Yeah, John.
**Participant:** Well, I just really appreciated the reminder, because I don't think of this very often, to pay attention to my state of mind when I give.
Whether I'm giving reluctantly or giving hoping to get something in particular back.
And so I really appreciate that.
